preamble: In Old English the Early West Saxon diphthong ie/īe, produced by i-mutation of ea/ēa and io/īo, typically appears as y/ȳ in Late West Saxon (ieldra > yldra, gelīefan > gelȳfan). Next to palatal consonants it became i instead (hīġ 'hay', niht 'night'). The phonetic value of EWS ie is disputed: proposals include [iy], [ie], [iə] or a single vowel between [i] and [e] (Quirk & Wrenn's 'unstable ĭ'). The change is limited to this one dialect.

examples.note: EWS ie from i-mutation of broken ea before l + consonant.
Long īe > ȳ; also spelled gelīfan in Alfredian texts.

sources: Campbell, A. (1959). Old English Grammar. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
